prompt: How do the stages of life shape our understanding of time and mortality?
answer:
The stages of life shape our sense of time by changing how much of it we remember, how much we expect, and what we feel we must do with it.

In childhood, time is often immediate and expansive. A summer can feel enormous because so much is new, and the future has few clear boundaries. Death may first appear as an absence—a person or animal who no longer returns—before it becomes understood as universal and irreversible.

In adolescence and early adulthood, time becomes a field of possibilities. We imagine different selves and futures, often feeling both impatient to begin and confident that there will be time. Mortality can be intellectually clear yet emotionally distant, though illness, loss, or danger can make it intimate much earlier.

In midlife, time often becomes more visibly finite. Raising children, watching parents age, or recognizing paths we will never take can shift the question from “What could I become?” to “What deserves the time I have?” Our own continuity becomes striking: inwardly, we may feel much the same while our bodies and circumstances register decades.

In later life, the past may occupy more attention, and the future may be measured less by distant milestones than by relationships, daily pleasures, or unfinished responsibilities. Mortality can provoke fear, acceptance, curiosity, or all three. A shorter horizon can make ordinary moments more precious, but it does not automatically bring peace or wisdom.

These are tendencies, not a universal sequence. Culture, health, faith, and especially early loss can alter them profoundly. At any age, mortality can make time feel scarce—or clarify what makes it worth inhabiting.

Perhaps the deepest change is that we gradually come to understand time as more than something that passes. It is the medium of attachment: people become irreplaceable because we have shared it, and choices matter because we cannot make every one. Mortality gives those limits their urgency, without telling us exactly how to live within them.
